design_detail: Inpatient, double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study in 6 people with cocaine dependence who were not seeking treatment. Each took part in five sessions over 7 to 10 days, one per day, receiving in randomized order cocaethylene 0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg, cocaine 0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg, or placebo, each dissolved in saline to 10 ml and injected intravenously over one minute, with doses calculated as free base. The randomization was constrained on the regulator's advice: the lower dose of either drug was always given before the higher dose of that drug. Participants lived on an inpatient unit throughout and were monitored for at least 24 hours before sessions began. Heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac rhythm were recorded from 30 minutes before to 180 minutes after dosing; visual analogue ratings from 30 minutes before to 120 minutes after; blood for cocaine and cocaethylene at 17 times out to 300 minutes. At the end of each session participants were asked to say which of four options they had received, as a check on blinding.
can_establish: In 6 people with cocaine dependence who used cocaine and alcohol together, how plasma concentrations, heart rate, systolic blood pressure and rated drug effects after intravenous cocaethylene at two doses compare, within the same people and under double-blind conditions, with the same doses of cocaine and with placebo.
cannot_establish: What cocaethylene does when it is formed inside the body from cocaine and alcohol rather than injected on its own (both parent drugs are then present); whether cocaethylene is more or less toxic than cocaine (no toxicity outcome was measured, and the sessions were in a monitored unit with exclusion of unwell participants); whether the absence of a difference on several measures means equivalence, in 6 people without a power calculation; or anything about people who use cocaine but not alcohol, or who use other routes.

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers recruited by newspaper advertisement in a US city; not seeking treatment (p. 154).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence and for alcohol abuse (2) or dependence (4) without physiological dependence, assessed by comprehensive medical and psychiatric evaluation including the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV; no other substance-related or mental disorders. Each signed a consent form approved by a university human investigations committee or a hospital human subjects committee, and the procedures followed national guidelines for giving drugs to humans. Study medication was withheld in any session in which heart rate exceeded 100 beats per minute, diastolic pressure 90 mmHg or systolic pressure 140 mmHg before dosing (pp. 154–155).
sample.demographics: Mean age 33 (SD 2.4) years; 5 men (3 Black American, 1 Caucasian, 1 Puerto Rican) and 1 woman (Black American) (p. 154).
sample.attrition: No losses are reported; all 6 appear in every analysis.
sample.selection_effects: A very small, highly selected group: people with cocaine dependence who also met criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence, who preferred crack cocaine, who were medically and psychiatrically screened, and who were not seeking treatment. Most had no previous experience of intravenous cocaine, which the authors raise as a reason why they could not reliably tell the drugs apart (p. 160). Reported use was heavy (mean 4.38 g of cocaine a week, with alcohol mainly during cocaine use, an average of 19 standard drinks a week), so the study doses are small relative to these participants' own use.

exposure.measurement: Drugs given in the laboratory and measured in plasma by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography with ion pairing, using cocaethylene as primary standard and n-propyl cocaine as internal standard, both synthesized from benzoylecgonine; coefficients of variation under 5% at 25 and 100 ng/ml (p. 155). Participants' own use was self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: cocaethylene 0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg, cocaine 0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg, or placebo (saline), in 10 ml injected intravenously over one minute, one condition per session, five sessions over 7 to 10 days, with doses calculated as free base (pp. 154–155). Self-reported own use: mean 4.38 (SD 1.2) g of cocaine a week, crack cocaine preferred, with alcohol consumed mainly during cocaine use at an average of 19 (8.2) standard drinks a week, a standard drink defined as 1.5 oz of liquor, 4 oz of wine or 12 oz of beer (p. 154).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol use was an entry criterion and defines the sample, but no alcohol was given in the study and no measure of recent drinking is reported for the inpatient period; other substance-related disorders were excluded by interview. Tobacco and caffeine use are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential throughout; clinically monitored for at least 24 hours before the first session, with sessions on separate days over 7 to 10 days (p. 155). No urine testing during the stay is described, and no measure of time since last use outside the unit is given.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant received all five conditions, including saline placebo and two matched doses of cocaine as the comparator for cocaethylene (p. 154).
comparison.matching: Within-person design; cocaethylene and cocaine were given at the same two mg/kg doses, calculated as free base, which the Discussion notes produced very similar plasma concentrations in this study, unlike the authors' earlier intranasal study (p. 159).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the between-drug comparison. For the cardiovascular and rated outcomes the pre-dose baseline in each session is the only reference point; tolerance from participants' own heavy use was not measured, and the constrained ascending dose order means any acute or session-to-session tolerance is confounded with dose.

outcomes.instruments: Heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac rhythm by automated monitor. Visual analogue scales for 'Any High', 'Rush', 'Stimulated', 'Sleepy', 'Paranoia', 'Sad/Depressed', 'Nervous', 'Good' and 'Bad' drug effects and 'I Want Cocaine', plus a participant-rated 'Cocaine High' scale of 0–100 mm anchored 0 = no effect, 25 = almost imperceptible, 50 = my usual, 75 = better than my usual effect, 100 = better than my best effect. Plasma cocaine and cocaethylene with non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (AUC by the linear trapezoidal rule extrapolated to infinity, half-life, clearance, steady-state volume of distribution, observed peak concentration). A four-option drug-identification question at the end of each session (pp. 154–155).
outcomes.validity_norms: The rating scales are the laboratory's standard instruments with a published source for the visual analogue format; the 'Cocaine High' anchors are self-referenced to the person's own usual effect, which makes them interpretable within a person but not comparable between people. Assay precision is reported; no norms apply.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Potency' is operationalized as the size of the change in heart rate, systolic pressure or a rating at a given mg/kg dose. Nothing is operationalized as toxicity or harm. Analyses used percentage change from the averaged pre-dose values for cardiovascular measures.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two-factor repeated-measures ANOVAs were run on heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure and ten or more ratings, with Student-Newman-Keuls post-hoc tests and P < 0.05 two-tailed; pharmacokinetic parameters were compared by paired t-tests (p. 155). Six ratings are reported only as showing nothing, with data not shown (p. 158).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind for participants and, by description, staff; blinding was checked by asking participants to name the drug afterwards, and their answers show the blind held poorly at the lower doses (p. 158). The assay and cardiovascular monitor are objective.

analysis.effect_sizes: F statistics with degrees of freedom and P values, and means with standard errors; no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes. Pharmacokinetics (Table 1, p. 155), cocaine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg against cocaethylene 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg: AUC 12 866 (SE 1957.30) and 28 628 (4598.16) against 16 329 (1299.17) and 34 106 (3192.98) ng.min/ml; half-life 91 (9.01) and 87 (7.19) against 149 (11.07) and 146 (9.49) minutes; clearance 0.021 (0.0028) and 0.019 (0.0024) against 0.015 (0.0014) and 0.015 (0.0015) l/min/kg; peak concentration 195 (57.11) and 444 (93.54) against 160 (40.53) and 329 (71.32) ng/ml. Compared with cocaine, cocaethylene showed slower clearance (P = 0.019), larger steady-state volume of distribution (P = 0.025) and longer terminal half-life (P = 0.0014), with AUC not significantly larger (P = 0.075) (p. 156). Heart rate: condition effect F = 12.37, df = 4, 25, P < 0.01, with cocaine 0.5 mg/kg above every other active condition (P < 0.02 to P < 0.05) and no difference between cocaine 0.25 mg/kg and either cocaethylene dose (P = 0.79 and P = 0.53). Systolic pressure: F = 4.43, df = 4, 25, P < 0.01, all conditions above placebo, no difference between active conditions. Ratings at 2.5 minutes (Table 2, p. 158), placebo against cocaine 0.25 and 0.5 and cocaethylene 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg: 'Cocaine High' 10 (6.3), 44.2 (9.7), 65.3 (7.9), 15.3 (6.6), 41.7 (5.43); 'Rush' 5 (4.6), 47.5 (10.1), 68.8 (4.3), 13.3 (8.2), 34.6 (8.5).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person ANOVAs on percentage change from baseline for cardiovascular measures.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned; the regulator required the ascending-dose constraint on the randomization (p. 155).
analysis.selective_reporting: Diastolic blood pressure and six ratings ('I Want Cocaine', 'Bad Drug Effects', 'Paranoia', 'Sad/Depressed', 'Nervous', 'Sleepy') are reported as showing nothing, with data not shown; the drug-identification results, the only check on blinding, are given in the text without a table (p. 158). Table 2 shows five ratings at a single time point each.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 6 participants, the repeated findings of no difference between cocaine 0.25 mg/kg and the two cocaethylene doses, and of no dose-response for cocaethylene on heart rate and systolic pressure, cannot be read as equivalence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At the same mg/kg dose and at similar plasma concentrations, cocaethylene raised heart rate less than cocaine (cocaine 0.5 mg/kg exceeded every other active condition) and produced lower ratings of 'Cocaine High', 'Any High', 'Rush', 'Stimulated' and 'Good Drug Effects'; cocaethylene 0.5 mg/kg produced effects that did not differ from cocaine 0.25 mg/kg, and cocaethylene 0.25 mg/kg did not differ from placebo on most ratings. Systolic pressure rose in every active condition with no difference between drugs or doses, and diastolic pressure showed no condition effect. Cocaethylene was cleared more slowly, with a terminal half-life around 146–149 minutes against 87–91 minutes for cocaine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion that cocaethylene has pharmacological properties in common with cocaine but is less potent is supported for heart rate and the rated effects at these doses; the equal effect on systolic pressure is reported alongside it. The Discussion goes further in two places. It states that the results of this and other studies indicate that cocaethylene alone is less toxic than cocaine (p. 160), though no toxicity outcome was measured here and the inference rests on potency on two cardiovascular measures and some ratings in 6 people. It also develops cocaethylene as a candidate substitution treatment for cocaine dependence (pp. 160–161), which is a proposal for future work rather than a finding, with the authors' own rodent studies cited as the basis. The claim that cocaethylene may contribute to toxicity when formed during combined use (abstract, p. 153; p. 160) likewise rests on its slower elimination rather than on anything measured here, and the authors state in the same paragraph that its effects cannot easily be separated from the combined effects of cocaine and alcohol.

timeline.event: Cocaethylene identified in blood after combined cocaine and ethanol use and shown to act at the dopamine transporter in rats and to maintain self-administration in monkeys
Perez-Reyes et al. (as cited here, p. 154): single-blind study of one intravenous cocaethylene dose (0.25 mg/kg), found less potent than an equivalent cocaine dose

McCance-Katz et al. (as cited here, pp. 154, 159): intranasal cocaethylene produced cocaine-like cardiovascular and rated effects but was less potent than cocaine, and had a longer elimination half-life
Multiple-dose study of concurrent cocaine and alcohol, cited here for the ratio of cocaethylene to cocaine exposure during combined use
Fractional conversion of intravenous cocaine to cocaethylene in people measured with labelled compounds (about 17% of the dose)

replication.where_it_stands: Three human studies in sequence, two of them from this group, now agree that cocaethylene given on its own is cocaine-like but less potent, and is eliminated more slowly. The open question is what this implies for combined cocaine and alcohol use: the paper reports from other work that the ratio of cocaethylene to cocaine exposure during combined use is about 0.2, so the concentrations reached here by injection are not those produced by the combination, and this study cannot say whether cocaethylene adds anything to the effects of cocaine and alcohol taken together.

funding.funder: Grants K20 DA00216, R29-09573 and P50 DA09250 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, and NIH-MO1-RR00125 from the US Public Health Service to a university general clinical research centre (p. 161).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from a university school of medicine's departments of psychiatry and laboratory medicine, a division of substance abuse and a veterans' healthcare system; the cocaethylene was supplied by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, which also funded the work (pp. 153–154). The same group had published the earlier intranasal study with which these results are compared, and was at the time starting work on cocaethylene as a possible substitution treatment (p. 161). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: For the question that matters to people who use cocaine with alcohol: a study in which cocaethylene is given to reach the concentrations actually produced by combined use, rather than the much higher ones reached here, with cardiac and hepatic outcomes rather than ratings; and, to separate the components, a factorial comparison of cocaine alone, alcohol alone, both together and cocaethylene alone, in the same people, with the order fully randomized rather than ascending.

domains.note: Order was randomized only within the constraint that the lower dose of each drug always preceded the higher, so dose is confounded with session order; the authors themselves raise this as a possible source of the cardiovascular tolerance they observed (p. 159). No allocation concealment or sequence-generation method is described, and no period or carry-over analysis is reported.

Conditions were double-blind and given on an inpatient unit, which limits outside use. The blind held poorly at lower doses: 5 of 6 experienced cocaine 0.25 mg/kg as cocaethylene, and cocaethylene 0.25 mg/kg was experienced as placebo by 3, so expectancy cannot be excluded for the ratings, though it works against rather than for the paper's main contrast.
All 6 participants completed all five sessions and appear in every reported analysis.

Plasma concentrations and cardiovascular measures are objective. The main subjective outcomes are single visual analogue ratings anchored to each person's own usual cocaine effect, and the 'Cocaine High' scale asks about a cocaine-specific experience in sessions where the drug was sometimes cocaethylene, which may itself pull ratings towards the familiar drug.

No protocol; fourteen or more outcomes analysed without correction; diastolic pressure, six ratings and the drug-identification data are reported without numbers; Table 2 contradicts the text on one result (see reporting issues); ratings are tabulated at a single time point.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 takes the overall judgment from the worst domain, and the ascending-dose constraint on the randomization is a genuine weakness: dose and session order are confounded in a design whose central claim is about relative potency at matched doses. Set against that, this is a double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person comparison with an objective assay, complete data, and plasma concentrations that turned out similar for the two drugs, which is what makes the potency comparison interpretable at all. Cite this source for cocaethylene given intravenously at 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg producing smaller increases in heart rate and lower ratings of high, rush and stimulation than the same doses of cocaine in 6 people with cocaine dependence; for similar rises in systolic pressure across all active conditions; and for cocaethylene's slower clearance and longer half-life. Do not cite it for cocaethylene being less toxic than cocaine, for its contribution to the effects or risks of combined cocaine and alcohol use, or for any statement about it as a treatment.

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene was eliminated more slowly than cocaine at the same doses: terminal half-life 149 (SE 11.07) and 146 (9.49) minutes for cocaethylene 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg against 91 (9.01) and 87 (7.19) minutes for cocaine; clearance 0.015 l/min/kg for both cocaethylene doses against 0.021 and 0.019 for cocaine; steady-state volume of distribution 2.93 and 2.74 against 2.40 and 1.94 l/kg.
key_findings.note: Tested as paired comparisons of cocaethylene against cocaine: clearance P = 0.019, volume of distribution P = 0.025, half-life P = 0.0014, AUC P = 0.075.

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations after the two drugs were similar at matched doses: peak concentration 160 (SE 40.53) and 329 (71.32) ng/ml for cocaethylene 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg against 195 (57.11) and 444 (93.54) ng/ml for cocaine, with cocaethylene AUC somewhat larger (16 329 and 34 106 against 12 866 and 28 628 ng.min/ml).
key_findings.note: This matters for the potency comparison: in the same authors' earlier intranasal study the equivalent cocaethylene dose had produced plasma concentrations twice those of cocaine (p. 159).

key_findings.finding: All four active conditions raised heart rate above placebo (P < 0.01), but cocaine 0.5 mg/kg raised it more than every other active condition (against cocaethylene 0.25 mg/kg P < 0.03, cocaethylene 0.5 mg/kg P < 0.05, cocaine 0.25 mg/kg P < 0.02), while cocaine 0.25 mg/kg and the two cocaethylene doses did not differ from one another (P = 0.79, P = 0.53) and the two cocaethylene doses did not differ (P = 0.71).
key_findings.locator: Results › Physiological effects, 1st paragraph; Fig. 4 (left panel)
key_findings.note: Condition effect F = 12.37, df = 4, 25, P < 0.01; baseline heart rate 72 (SE 0.6) beats per minute. For the three conditions that did not differ, the maximum change was about 20% above baseline, 2.5 to 10 minutes after dosing (p. 159).

key_findings.finding: Systolic blood pressure rose above placebo in all four active conditions (P < 0.05) with no significant differences between them, and no condition effect was found for diastolic pressure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Physiological effects, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 4 (right panel)
key_findings.note: Condition effect for systolic pressure F = 4.43, df = 4, 25, P < 0.01; baseline 123 (SE 0.6) mmHg; the two cocaine doses compared gave P = 0.09. Diastolic data are not shown.

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene 0.25 mg/kg did not differ from placebo on 'Cocaine High' (P = 0.64), 'Any High' (P = 0.45), 'Rush' (P = 0.77) or 'Stimulated' (P = 0.45), while cocaethylene 0.5 mg/kg exceeded placebo on each of these and did not differ from cocaine 0.25 mg/kg on 'Cocaine High' (P = 0.24) or 'Rush' (P = 0.14).
Cocaine 0.5 mg/kg produced higher ratings than cocaethylene 0.5 mg/kg on 'Cocaine High' (P < 0.01) and 'Rush' (P < 0.01), while on 'Stimulated' the two did not differ significantly (P = 0.12).

Blinding held poorly at the lower doses: when given cocaine 0.25 mg/kg, 5 of 6 participants said they had received cocaethylene and 1 identified cocaine; cocaethylene 0.25 mg/kg was experienced as placebo by 3, as cocaethylene by 2 and as cocaine by 1; cocaine 0.5 mg/kg was correctly identified by 5 of 6 and cocaethylene 0.5 mg/kg by 4 of 6; placebo was correctly identified by 4 of 6.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective effects, last two paragraphs
key_findings.note: Reported in the text only, with data not shown; the authors' preferred explanation is that cocaine 0.25 mg/kg and both cocaethylene doses produced effects too similar to tell apart (p. 160).

key_findings.finding: Plotting 'Cocaine High' against plasma concentration over time produced a clockwise loop for both drugs, which the authors read as acute tolerance or rapid distribution to the brain, while heart rate first showed a counter-clockwise loop, read as a lag in distribution, followed by a weaker sign of tolerance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics, last paragraph; Figs 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Descriptive plots of group means with no statistical test; the authors note the loop shape can also be explained by distribution alone (p. 160).

key_findings.finding: Repeated-measures analyses of 'I Want Cocaine', 'Bad Drug Effects', 'Paranoia', 'Sad/Depressed', 'Nervous' and 'Sleepy' showed no statistically significant findings.
key_findings.note: Data not shown; with 6 participants these null results are uninformative about whether such effects differ between the drugs.

key_findings.finding: The participants were 6 people with DSM-IV cocaine dependence who were not seeking treatment, 5 men and 1 woman, mean age 33 (SD 2.4), all using cocaine and alcohol concurrently with crack cocaine preferred, reporting a mean of 4.38 (SD 1.2) g of cocaine and 19 (8.2) standard drinks a week, with alcohol drunk mainly during cocaine use.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks cocaethylene 0.5 mg/kg with an asterisk for 'Good Drug Effect' (43.3, SE 9.0), the asterisk denoting a significant difference from placebo at P < 0.05, while the text states that this effect was not statistically significant (P = 0.06).
reporting_issues.consequence: A direct table-text contradiction on whether the higher cocaethylene dose increased ratings of good drug effect above placebo. The text's P value should be preferred, and this cell of Table 2 should not be cited as significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Every ANOVA is reported with df = 4, 25, which corresponds to 30 independent observations. For five conditions given to the same 6 people, a repeated-measures analysis has df = 4, 20; the printed degrees of freedom are those of a between-subjects analysis of the same 30 session means.
reporting_issues.consequence: The error term may not account for the within-person design. Recomputing the printed F statistics at df = 4, 20 (editors' calculation) leaves every reported effect significant at P < 0.05 (for example heart rate P = 0.00003 instead of 0.00001, 'Good Drug Effects' P = 0.027 instead of 0.022), so the conclusions do not change, but the post-hoc comparisons rest on the same error term and the printed P values are slightly optimistic.

reporting_issues.issue: Baseline values are given as 72 (0.6) beats per minute and 123 (0.6) mmHg, described as means with standard errors across the five conditions; a standard error of 0.6 across 6 people on separate days is implausibly small for between-person variation and must describe the spread of the five condition means rather than of participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: The baseline figures cannot be used as estimates of these participants' resting heart rate or blood pressure, only as evidence that the pre-dose values were similar across conditions.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Table 2 states that ratings were measured at 2.5 minutes and at 15 minutes for 'Good Drug Effect', while the text states that 'Good Drug Effects' were collected at five time points (baseline, 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes after dosing) and does not say which is tabulated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The time point behind the 'Good Drug Effect' row of Table 2 is ambiguous, and the time course of that rating cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV is cited in the text as First et al. 1995 and in the reference list as First et al. 1996.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial for interpretation; noted because the instrument version matters when comparing diagnostic criteria across studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The only data on whether blinding held are reported in prose, with 'data not shown'; diastolic blood pressure and six of the rating scales are likewise reported without numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The integrity of the double blind cannot be quantified, and the null findings on paranoia, bad drug effects, craving and the others cannot be re-used or pooled.
